subject: Environment
topic: Green building and sustainable construction — mixed tiers
description: GRIHA, LEED-India, IGBC, energy efficiency, ECBC norms, embodied energy

questions.stem: GRIHA — India's national green building rating system — was developed by:

options.option_text: BIS and CPCB
TERI in association with the Ministry of New and Renewable Energy (MNRE)
ISRO and IIT Delhi
World Bank

questions.explanation: GRIHA — Green Rating for Integrated Habitat Assessment — developed by The Energy and Resources Institute (TERI) jointly with MNRE in 2007. Adopted as the national rating system in November 2009. Rated on a scale of 1-5 stars across 34 criteria (sustainable site, water, energy, materials, IEQ, innovation). Mandatory for several categories of central government projects. International peers: LEED (USGBC, USA), BREEAM (UK), CASBEE (Japan).

questions.stem: The IGBC (Indian Green Building Council) is a part of:

options.option_text: Ministry of Environment, Forest & Climate Change
CII (Confederation of Indian Industry)
FICCI
Bureau of Indian Standards

questions.explanation: IGBC — formed by CII (Sohrabji Godrej Green Business Centre) in 2001. Awards LEED-India ratings (in collaboration with USGBC) — Certified, Silver, Gold, Platinum. Multiple sub-categories: New Construction, Existing Buildings (O&M), Schools, Healthcare, Homes, Cities, Townships, Net Zero Energy. India ranks 3rd globally in number of LEED-certified projects (behind US, China). Famous certified projects: CII-Sohrabji Godrej GBC Hyderabad (world's first LEED Platinum building outside USA, 2003).

questions.stem: The Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC) — applicable to commercial buildings with connected load ≥ 100 kW or contract demand ≥ 120 kVA — is enforced by the:

options.option_text: MoEFCC
Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE)
RBI
MNRE

questions.explanation: ECBC — first launched 2007, revised 2017 — sets minimum energy-efficiency standards for commercial buildings. Categories: ECBC, ECBC+, Super-ECBC. Administered by BEE under the Ministry of Power (BEE was set up under the Energy Conservation Act, 2001). 26 states have notified ECBC; states adapt for local climate (5 climatic zones). Eco-Niwas Samhita (2018, 2021) is the residential version targeting domestic envelope efficiency.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a typical feature of a green building?

options.option_text: Rainwater harvesting
Use of locally-sourced materials
Heavy reliance on imported PVC and aluminium
Daylight harvesting + low-VOC paints

questions.explanation: Green buildings minimise embodied energy by AVOIDING long-haul / high-energy-intensive materials. Aluminium has very high embodied energy (~227 MJ/kg). PVC is petroleum-based with toxic additives (phthalates). Both are usually substituted with bamboo, timber, fly-ash bricks, ferrocement, recycled-content steel. Other green-building features — passive solar design, green roofs, solar PV/water, low-flow fixtures, greywater recycling, EV charging, native landscaping (xeriscaping).

questions.stem: The 'Urban Heat Island' effect, mitigated through green-building practices, refers to:

options.option_text: Cooler temperatures in cities than rural areas
Higher temperatures (typically 2-7 °C) in urbanised areas vs surrounding rural areas, due to dense built-up surfaces and reduced vegetation
Volcanic activity beneath cities
Elevated humidity in coastal cities

questions.explanation: UHI — concrete, asphalt, dark roofs absorb solar radiation by day and re-radiate heat at night. Reduced tree cover → less evapotranspiration cooling. Anthropogenic heat (vehicles, AC exhausts) adds. Mitigation: cool roofs (high-albedo), green roofs, urban afforestation, shaded pavements, reflective paints (SRI > 78), permeable surfaces. Indian cities like Delhi, Hyderabad, Ahmedabad have begun adopting Heat Action Plans; Ahmedabad's HAP (2013) was India's first.

questions.stem: 'Embodied energy' of a building material refers to:

options.option_text: Energy released when the material burns
Total energy used in extraction, processing, manufacture and transport of the material
Operational energy of the building's HVAC
Solar energy stored in the material

questions.explanation: Embodied energy — 'cradle-to-site' or 'cradle-to-grave' energy footprint. Per kg approximate values: timber ~2 MJ; brick ~3 MJ; concrete ~1.1 MJ; steel ~25-32 MJ; aluminium ~227 MJ; carbon fibre ~286 MJ. Strategies to lower: use locally-sourced low-energy materials (mud, bamboo, fly-ash), recycle/reuse (recycled steel uses 75% less energy than virgin), choose materials with high durability so the embodied energy is amortised over a longer life.

questions.stem: India's first 'Net Zero Energy' building (commercial scale) — built by BEE in New Delhi — is named:

options.option_text: Indira Paryavaran Bhawan
TERI Retreat, Gurgaon
Suzlon One Earth, Pune
Infosys Pocharam

questions.explanation: Indira Paryavaran Bhawan (the MoEFCC headquarters, New Delhi, inaugurated 25 February 2014) — India's first Net Zero Energy commercial building. Features: 930 kWp rooftop solar PV, geothermal cooling, atrium for daylighting, GRIHA 5-star + LEED Platinum. Generates more energy than it consumes annually. Other notable green buildings — CII-Godrej GBC Hyderabad (1st LEED Platinum, 2003), Suzlon One Earth (Pune, LEED Platinum + GRIHA 5), Infosys Pocharam, Hyderabad.

questions.stem: The LEED green building certification programme is administered globally by which organisation?

options.option_text: US Green Building Council (USGBC), based in Washington DC
World Green Building Council, headquartered in London
United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), Nairobi
Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE), Ministry of Power

questions.explanation: LEED (Leadership in Energy and Environmental Design) is owned and administered by the US Green Building Council (USGBC), a private non-profit body headquartered in Washington DC. Many candidates confuse it with the World Green Building Council (WorldGBC), which is a separate umbrella federation that does not itself award LEED certification. BEE administers India-specific energy programmes, not LEED.

questions.stem: In green building water-management practice, 'greywater' refers to wastewater originating from which source?

options.option_text: Toilets and urinals carrying human waste and pathogens
Stormwater collected from rooftops and paved external areas
Sinks, showers, and laundry - suitable for recycled reuse
Industrial effluent from manufacturing and chemical processes

questions.explanation: Greywater is lightly contaminated wastewater from baths, showers, hand-wash basins, and laundry. It is free of faecal matter and can be treated and reused for toilet flushing or irrigation, reducing freshwater demand. Wastewater from toilets is called 'blackwater' and requires full sewage treatment. Stormwater is classified separately as runoff water, not greywater.

questions.stem: A higher 'Window-to-Wall Ratio' (WWR) in a commercial building envelope generally results in which of the following outcomes?

options.option_text: Reduced solar heat gain through the building envelope in all climates
Increased solar heat gain and glare, raising the cooling energy demand
Greater thermal mass, helping stabilise indoor temperatures overnight
Improved acoustic insulation owing to the larger glass surface area

questions.explanation: WWR is the ratio of total glazed area to the gross exterior wall area. In hot climates like most of India, a higher WWR increases solar heat gain and glare, directly raising air-conditioning loads. This is why ECBC caps WWR (typically ≤ 40 % for non-north facades). Option A is wrong because glass transmits more solar radiation than opaque walls. Glass has very low thermal mass (option C is wrong), and glass has inferior acoustic performance compared to concrete or brick walls (option D is wrong).

questions.stem: Fly ash bricks are considered more environmentally sustainable than traditional fired clay bricks primarily because they:

options.option_text: Are fired at lower kiln temperatures, reducing fuel consumption by half
Contain embedded natural lime, acting as carbon-sequestering materials
Have lower density, directly reducing structural load on foundations
Reuse coal combustion waste and require no high-temperature kiln firing

questions.explanation: Fly ash bricks are made from fly ash (a coal-power-plant waste), lime, gypsum, and sand, and are cured using steam or autoclaving — not kiln firing. This diverts industrial waste from landfills and eliminates the high-temperature firing step that makes clay brick production energy-intensive and soil-degrading. Option A is wrong because fly ash bricks bypass kiln firing entirely, not merely use lower temperatures. Option B is incorrect because they are not carbon-sequestering in a meaningful sense. Option C (density advantage) is a secondary benefit, not the primary environmental reason.

questions.stem: The Bureau of Energy Efficiency (BEE) 'Star Rating Programme' for buildings evaluates and compares building performance using which primary metric?

options.option_text: Energy Use Intensity (EUI) measured in kWh per sq. m. per year
Total installed capacity of on-site renewable energy systems in kW
Proportion of green-certified construction materials used (by cost)
GRIHA composite score combined with occupant comfort survey ratings

questions.explanation: BEE's Star Rating Programme (launched 2009 for office buildings, later expanded) rates a building from 1 to 5 stars based on its Energy Performance Index (EPI), a form of Energy Use Intensity — annual energy consumption divided by the conditioned floor area (kWh/sq.m./year). Lower EPI = more stars. Option B confuses it with renewable capacity targets. Options C and D describe GRIHA criteria, not BEE's star rating methodology.

questions.stem: Under India's Energy Conservation Building Code (ECBC), the prescribed 'Overall Thermal Transfer Value' (OTTV) limit governs heat gain through which specific building element?

options.option_text: Roof assembly including insulation, waterproofing, and reflective coating
Ground-floor slab and sub-surface basement walls contacting the earth
Vertical envelope — opaque exterior walls and fenestration (glazing) combined
Mechanical HVAC ductwork passing through unconditioned building spaces

questions.explanation: ECBC defines OTTV as a composite index of heat gain through the vertical building envelope — both opaque walls and windows/glazing together. A separate metric, RTTV (Roof Thermal Transfer Value), covers the roof. This distinction is a frequent examination trap: candidates often assume OTTV covers roofs as well. Options B and D are not metrics addressed by OTTV at all. The ECBC limits OTTV to 45 W/m² for most climate zones, encouraging low-SHGC glass and external shading.

questions.stem: India's 'ECO Niwas Samhita' (ENS) 2018 is legislatively significant because it is India's first energy conservation code specifically designed for which building sector?

options.option_text: Government office buildings with a connected load exceeding 100 kW
Residential buildings and housing complexes with standardised energy norms
Large commercial retail complexes with built-up area above 500 sq. m.
Industrial production facilities with high process-heat energy demands

questions.explanation: ENS 2018, notified under the Energy Conservation Act 2001, is India's first dedicated energy code for the residential sector, covering apartments and plotted housing. The ECBC (which preceded it) covers only commercial buildings. ENS sets norms for building envelope, lighting, and appliances in homes. Option A describes the ECBC applicability threshold (500 kW connected load for commercial buildings, not 100 kW for government offices). Options C and D fall under ECBC's commercial and industrial domains respectively. ENS was a landmark because the residential sector accounts for roughly 25% of India's total electricity consumption.
